doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: Leaving Elizabeth City for Howard and meeting Baraka
summary: Decided to be a poet; left for Howard in 1952 for pre-med, met LeRoi Jones, and the hat story. Acting in He Who Gets Slapped; committed to poetry by junior year.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well let’s talk about your poetry for a bit. I wonder first of all do you decide, as a young man, to be a poet?
I decided to be a poet when I was in college.
And is that something, from a practical sense, that you felt you could make a living at?

No. Not at all. I did not at all think about making a living. I just thought that I wanted to write. I didn’t want — I left home, left Elizabeth City, North Carolina in 1952 to go to Howard University to study to be pre-med. The high school I went to in Elizabeth City was really very poor and extremely easy for me. I didn’t even take my books home at night and I was valedictorian. So when I got to college there I was without a study habit to my name and I really bombed out in pre-med you know because I really did not have any sense about how to be a student and I was the kind of student who read everything but what he was assigned. I met LeRoi Jones Baraka when I went there. I mean it was kind of funny I remember the day I met him I had just arrived and I had this outfit that I had shopped all year for to go to Howard. And it was basically a Zoot suit but except it was a sport coat and pants and the shoulders were out to here, this huge lapel tapered all the way down to the crotch to a tight-fitting waist. The pants flared out 14 inches at the

thigh and nine inches at the cuff and it was a blue and white herringbone jacket against a powder blue pair of pants with one dark blue stitch going down the side which sort of pulled the outfit together, and a pair of alligator suede wingtips. And I knew I was sharp. And I got to campus and everybody’s in Brooks Brothers. Or it might not have been Brooks Brothers, it might have been, I don’t know, J. Crew or whatever cheaper versions of it are but I was immediately out of place. And that’s what I was wearing when I met Baraka. And I had this hat — we got to be friends, I don’t know why because he was a year ahead of me, I don’t know why he took me in but he did. And I had this hat that I thought was wonderful. But he hated it. And one drunken night he snatched my hat and ran across campus and threw it in the reservoir. And so in other words you know you can’t dress like this and hang out with me was the basic message. So at any rate, no so my college years are like everybody’s college years, wonderful and a case of a way of finding myself and growing up. But it soon became apparent to me that I wanted to live a more creative life. I was always attracted to the creative offerings that the school had — the theater group, now I joined the theater company, the Howard Players I had a lead role in “He Who Gets Slapped.” And there was a time that I was reading existentialism and I’m reading Sartre and Camus and Kierkegaard and dying to find people to use it on. I had this one line where the guy says “Who are you?” And my line was, “I am he who gets slapped.” But I had decided for some weird Kierkegaardian reason that it wasn’t “he who gets slapped” but it was “he who gets slapped.” I had a very profound explanation for this. I remember Mr. Dawson, the director, said, “No, Spellman, that’s not the line. You say, ‘I am he who gets slapped.’” I said, “No but you realize that with issues of reunification and the self and I started going on. He said, “Look you’re not a theater major, I have many theater majors who would like to have this part, you can say, ‘I am he who gets slapped’ or in about five minutes more these theater majors are going to have the part.” So but anyway it was, you know, utterly pretentious college student. But even in the course of all that pretention you do learn and you do grow and you do think a lot about things. But by my junior year I was really fully committed to being a poet.
